In-situ microaeration of anaerobic digester treating buffalo manure for
enhanced biogas yield

a b s t r a c t
Microaeration pretreatment can enhance lignin degradation of lignocellulosic biomass and subsequent
biogas production during anaerobic digestion (AD). However, the reported values of effective aeration
dose, aeration contact time, and aeration frequency differ with substrates riddling the selection of a
suitable combination. A serial approach was adopted to identify the suitable combination for the
degradation of lignin in the buffalo manure and improvement of the biogas production. Single and
Multiple injections of three aeration doses of 5.3, 7.3, and 9.3 mL O2/g VS were tested at 5 different
contact timese 6, 12, 24, 36, and 47 h. Results for acid-soluble lignin (% ASL) indicated the suitability of
12 h contact time with a single injection of 7.3 mL O2/g VS for lignin degradation and biogas enhance-
ment for AD of buffalo manure. This combination achieved 78% higher ASL content and a 32% increase in
average daily biogas yield than the control. Finally, the kinetic parameters obtained through the modiﬁed
Gompertz model accurately predicted the biogas potential of the process (R2 > 0.93). The results of this
study can be referenced for improving the yield of similar biomass to bioenergy initiatives by employing
a low-cost pretreatment strategy of in-situ microaeration.

1. Introduction
Animal manure laden with pollutants including antibiotic resi-
dues, hormones, and heavy metals is produced in abundance in
developing countries [1]. A large amount of this waste is left un-
treated resulting in environmental pollution as well as a loss of a
valuable resource [2]. Anaerobic digestion (AD) can effectively
reduce the environmental harmfulness of organic waste [3] and
simultaneously produce the much-needed bioenergy in the form of
biogas [4]. Animal waste, even after the loss of nutrients in the
animal gut, has enough nutrients that make it a low-cost input with
valuable outputs through the AD process [5]. However, being
lignocellulosic, the presence of lignin renders low efﬁciency to the
AD of lignocellulosic biomass [6]).
Lignocellulosic biomass is composed of 20e50% cellulose,
15e35% hemicellulose, and 18e35% lignin [7]. During fermentation,
the major portion of sugars is derived from the cellulosic part of
lignocellulosic biomass, which is then converted into fuels and
chemicals [8]. Both cellulose and hemicellulose interwound to form
a network of ﬁbers where lignin gets impregnated to form strong

cemented linkages in biomass. Lignin is a complex polymer made of
aromatic alcohols (phenols) that makes it difﬁcult to hydrolyze
during AD [9]. Thus, the limited biodegradation of lignocellulosic
biomass is one of the key challenges to AD [10].
The ﬁrst step in the multi-step AD process is the hydrolysis of
polymers [11]. For lignocellulosic biomass, hydrolysis is the rate-
limiting step for the AD process [12]. Thus animal wastes contain-
ing higher lignin content will give limited bioenergy through
conventional AD [13] due to the high content of hardly degradable
lignocellulosic content in the feedstock [14]. Application of a suit-
able biomass pretreatment method for lignin removal before AD
can, therefore, enhance the efﬁciency and increase the biogas
production [15]. Table 1 summarizes a variety of biomass pre-
treatment methodse physical, chemical, and biologicald that are
commonly practiced these days.
It can be seen in Table 1 that each pretreatment method has its
pros and cons and, no single method is advantaged over the other.
For example, physical methods cannot disrupt the lignocellulosic
structure, chemical processes require complex technical knowledge
for smooth operation or else they will pose a risk to the process and
the equipment, and ﬁnally, the biological processes are too slow to
be adopted. Thus, choosing an effective pretreatment method is not
an easy task. Recently, microaeration of the substrate for disrupting
the lignocellulosic structure is reported as an effective pretreat-
ment method requiring minimal ﬁnancial and technical resources
(Cesaro & Belgiorno, 2014; [8,19].
The introduction of small amounts of oxygen in the anaerobic
digester has been described as a low-cost and effective strategy to
promote the hydrolysis efﬁciency of the process [20,21]. Injecting
small amounts of oxygen (microaeration) in the anaerobic digester
is found to be an effective in-situ biomass pretreatment method
that facilitates the growth of microbes and stimulates hydrolysis of
complex organic matter [8]. Initially, microaeration was used for
biogas up-gradation by desulphurization of biogas, but now it is
also utilized for improving the hydrolysis and methanogenesis step
of AD [22]). [23]; found positive effects of micro-aerated anaerobic
digestion system on facultative microbes such as Firmicutes and
Clostridia resulting in a better hydrolysis rate. Similarly, the meth-
anogenic step was also improved because of the prevalence of aero-
tolerant Methanosarcina and Methanobacterium spp. in the micro-
aerated anaerobic digester.
The positive effects of the microaeration pretreatment to ach-
ieve enhanced hydrolytic rates during the AD process have been
reported AD of wastewater [24,25], black water [26], food waste
[19,27], energy crops (Kaparaju et al., 2009), and agricultural resi-
dues [8,28,29]. Previous literature identiﬁes three common varia-
blese aeration dose, aeration contact time, and aeration frequency
that play the dominant role in the effectiveness of microaeration
pretreatment for an efﬁcient AD process. However, the diversity of
substrates and the associated disparity of the suitable parameters
used in available literature makes it challenging to achieve the
positive effects of microaeration [30]. Another important yet
understudied effect of microaeration pretreatment is on lignin
degradation. In the case of lignocellulosic biomass, hydrolysis is the
rate-limiting step, and the efﬁciency of a pretreatment process is
signiﬁcantly dependent on the degradation of lignin. The degra-
dation of lignin signiﬁcantly improves the availability of sugars for
microbial consumption which ultimately leads to better biogas
yield. Finally, administering an improper amount of oxygen can be
inhibitory rather than beneﬁcial for the methanogens [21]. Thus,
the availability of congruous data can increase the adaptability of
the low-cost in-situ pretreatment strategies like microaeration
particularly in low-income countries where cost is the governing
factor in decision making.
AD of buffalo manure is one of the most feasible bioenergy
production processes in developing countries like Pakistan. Buffalo
is a common domestic animal in Pakistan reared for milk and meat
and its waste is often added to ﬁelds as fertilizer. In few instances
where AD is practiced in Pakistan, the primary substrate is buffalo
waste. It is estimated that there is a potential of 16.3 million m3 per
day biogas production in Pakistan that can cater to the energy
needs of almost 112 million residents of rural areas [31]. However,
quantitative ﬂuctuation in gas production has largely hindered the
adoption of this process in Pakistan [32]. Therefore, ﬁnding a cost-
effective and technically simple biomass pretreatment method is
imperative to enhance the biogas yield from the manure AD pro-
cess and to increase its popularity and adaptability in developing
countries. This study is aimed at determining the speciﬁc aeration
dose, contact time, and aeration frequency for efﬁcient degradation
of lignin present in the buffalo manure for subsequent improve-
ment of biogas production during the AD process.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Substrate and inoculum
Fresh ‘as excreted’ buffalo manure was collected and used as the
substrate for this research. Fresh manure samples were taken from
nearby farms in district Abbottabad. After collection, the substrate
was stored at 4 C until used in the experiment. The inoculum used
in this study was taken from already operating lab scale digesters.
Before its use in the experiments, the inoculum was stored under
anaerobic conditions until the gas production stopped. The physi-
cochemical characteristics of substrate and inoculum are shown in

2.2. Experimental setup
The whole experiment was divided into two phases to achieve
the overall objective of the study.
2.2.1. Phase-I
Phase-I of this study was used to screen out the best aeration
dose, aeration contact time, and frequency of aeration. Initial values
for these parameters were selected based on the available litera-
ture. The outcome of this phase was measured as the decrease in
the amount of acid-soluble lignin (ASL) as compared to control.
Accordingly, three sets of screening experiments were performed.
In each experiment,10 g of the substrate was added in a 60 mL glass
bottle and ﬂushed with nitrogen for up to 3 min, and sealed
immediately to make it airtight. Afterward, the gases were evacu-
ated, and a speciﬁed amount of air (as mentioned in Table 3) was
injected into the digesters. The treatments were run in triplicates
and the performance was measured against control bottles con-
taining unaerated substrates.
During experiment 1, the efﬁcacy of 7.3 mL O2/g VS aeration
dose was tested at 5 levels of timed 6 h,12 h, 24 h, 36 h, and 47 h to
select the best contact time for lignin degradation. The initial se-
lection of 7.3 mL O2/g VS aeration dose was based on the previous
tests conducted with this dose using a lignocellulosic substrate
with a similar biochemical composition [23,29]. After identifying a
suitable contact time for aeration, experiment 2 tested the efﬁcacy
of three levels of aeration dosesd 5.3 mL O2/g VS, 7.3 mL O2/g VS,
and 9.3 mL O2/g VS at two levels of timed 12 h and 24 h to select
the best aeration dose for lignin degradation. Finally, experiment 3a
and experiment 3b further elucidated the effect of pulse aeration on
lignin degradation at 12 h and 24 h aeration contact time. The
summary of the experimental design and conditions for the ex-
periments are shown in Table 3.
2.2.2. Phase-II
Phase-II of this study aimed at ﬁnding the effectiveness of
aeration pretreatment on enhancing biogas yield during batch
anaerobic digestion of the buffalo manure. Manure samples added
in triplicate 1-L bottle-reactors (600 mL effective volume) were ﬁrst
aerated with a single aeration dose of 7.3 mL O2/g VS for 12 h (based
on the ﬁndings of screening experiments: phase-I). Afterward, the
anaerobic inoculum was added to each digester to achieve a sub-
strate to inoculum ratio of 1 on a volatile solid basis. All the reactors
were ﬂushed with nitrogen for 3e5 min to create anaerobic con-
ditions and sealed immediately. The digesters were placed in a
water bath at 35 ± 2 C for 14 d to mimic the mesophilic AD process.
The digestion was stopped at day 14 since the data for biogas
production for both the control and treatments did not show any
signiﬁcant change in daily biogas production beyond day 10. The
digesters were manually shaken for 10 min every day to obtain
thorough mixing. Following the same protocol, triplicate 1-L bottle-
reactors containing unaerated manure samples and inoculum were
used as control. Background biogas produced by the inoculum was
measured under the same conditions and adjusted for the other
biogas digesters.
2.3. Analytical methods
Total solids, volatile solids, chemical oxygen demand, pH, and
NH4eN of the substrate and inoculum were measured according to
the standard methods (APHA, 1998). The standard NREL method
(National Renewable Energy Laboratory) was used for the deter-
mination of lignin content in lignocellulosic biomass [35]). The
spectrophotometric method was used to estimate total phenolic
content (TPC) as explained by [36]. Brieﬂy, 1 mL extract was mixed
with 5 mL of diluted Folin Ciocalteu followed by mixing of 4 mL
Na2CO3 solution (7.5%). The mixture was incubated at room tem-
perature in dark for 90min and absorbance was measured at
760 nm. Measured levels of TPC were stated as mg Gallic acid
equivalents in 100g of the fresh sample (mg GAE/100g, FW). Biogas
produced in each digester was removed daily with the help of a
50 mL syringe and quantiﬁed. The measured wet biogas volume
was then adjusted for standard temperature (0 C) and pressure
(1atm) according to equation (1) as described in [37].

2.4. Statistical analysis
The outputs of the experiments were statistically analyzed by
single-factor analysis of variance (1-way ANOVA) using Minitab
software version 16 at a ¼ 0.05. When the results of ANOVA showed
a signiﬁcant difference, the means were further compared using
Post-hoc Tukey's test [37].
2.5. Kinetic study
The reliability of the experimental data obtained for cumulative
biogas yield is widely ensured by ﬁtting the data into the Gompertz
kinetic model [38]. Thus, a modiﬁed Gompertz model (Equation
(2)) was used in this study to ﬁt the kinetics of biogas production
during batch AD of aerated and un-aerated buffalo manure. The
simulation results provide insightful information about the AD
process by predicting lag time, biogas production potential, tech-
nical digestion time, and maximum biogas production rate of the
anaerobic digestion process.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Inﬂuence of microaeration pretreatment on lignin degradation
For phase I, a sequence of three screening experiments was
conducted to identify the best combination of aeration contact
time, aeration dose, and aeration frequency to achieve maximum
lignin degradation measured as percent acid-soluble lignin (% ASL)
of the substrate biomass. During experiment 1, the substrate was
aerated at ﬁve levels of contact time while injecting all digesters
with 7.3 mL O2/g VS of the substrate to identify the aeration contact
time that achieves maximum lignin degradation of the substrate.
Fig. 1 shows the results of experiment 1 of phase I for lignin
degradation in the substrate.
It can be seen in Fig.1 that the digester injected with 7.3 mL O2/g
VS of the substrate and 12 h contact time contained only 3.96%
acid-soluble lignin (ASL) degrading 78% more ASL as compared to
control (initial ASL content of 17.09%) followed by 77% ASL degra-
dation at 24 h, 68% ASL degradation at 36 h, 60% ASL degradation at
47 h, and only 4.5% ASL degradation at 6 h. Thus, based on this
ﬁnding 12 h was identiﬁed as the best aeration contact time for
deligniﬁcation using a single injection of 7.3 mL O2/g VS of the
substrate. Furthermore, to identify the best aeration dose, experi-
ment 2 of phase I was carried out with 24 h and 12 h of aeration
contact time. Since the results of lignin degradation achieved at
12 h and 24 h were not signiﬁcantly different (a ¼ 0.05) both
contact times were further tested in experiment 2. Previous studies
have also reported the suitability of 12 h and 24 h aeration contact
time for biomass aeration pretreatment and subsequent improve-
ment in biogasiﬁcation through anaerobic digestion [23,33,34].
Fig. 2 shows the results of experiment 2 of phase I where three
aeration dosesd5.3 mL O2/g VS, 7.3 mL O2/g VS, and 9.3 mL O2/g VS
of the substrate were tested for their deligniﬁcation ability.
The results revealed that aeration dose of 7.3 mL O2/g VS dose
was most effective in lignin degradation among three tested aera-
tion doses. Accordingly, 7.3 mL O2/g VS aeration dose resulted in
higher lignin degradation for 12 h aeration contact time compared
to 24 h. For 12 h aeration contact time, 7.3 mL O2/g VS dose resulted
in 3.96% ASL content which was 68% lower than the 5.3 mL O2/g VS
dose (12.32% ASL) and 75% lower than the 9.3 mL O2/g VS dose
(15.61% ASL). Similarly, for 24 h aeration contact time, 7.3 mL O2/g
VS dose resulted in 4.12% ASL content which was 71% lower than
the 5.3 mL O2/g VS dose (14.31% ASL) and 65% lower than the 9.3 mL
O2/g VS dose (11.93% ASL). Thus, the results of experiment 2 depict
that 12 h of aeration contact time with a single injection of 7.3 mL
O2/g VS aeration dose caused maximum degradation of lignin.
Finally, experiment 3 was conducted to study the effect of aeration
frequency on lignin degradation. For this, multiple doses of 7.3 mL
O2/g VS were injected in the respective digesters during 12 h and
24 h contact times (Table 3). For single aeration, 7.3 mL O2/g VS was
injected in the respective digesters at the beginning of the exper-
iment. Whereas, for multiple aerations, 7.3 mL O2/g VS was injected
in the respective digesters at 0 h, 1 h, and 6 h during 12 h contact
time, and for 24 h contact time 7.3 mL O2/g VS was injected at 0 h,
1 h, and 12 h.
Fig. 3 shows the results of experiment 3 of this study.
It is clear in Fig. 3 that increasing the frequency of aeration did
not signiﬁcantly affect the lignin degradation both at 12 h and 24 h
contact times. For 12 h contact time, three doses of 7.3 mL O2/g VS
air were injected in the respective digesters at 0 h, 1 h, and 6 h that
resulted in 16.91% ASL which was not signiﬁcantly different than
control (17.09% ASL). Similarly, for 24 h contact time, three doses of
7.3 mL O2/g VS air were injected in the respective digesters at 0 h,
1 h, and 12 h that resulted in 16.89% ASL which was again not
signiﬁcantly different than control (17.09% ASL). Thus, injection of a
single dose of 7.3 mL O2/g VS for 12 h and 24 h was deemed suitable
to degrade the lignin in the substrate resulting in 3.96% ASL for 12 h
contact time and 4.12% ASL for 24 h contact time.
[33] suggested improved hydrolysis of lignocellulosic biomass
when microaerobically pretreated before the anaerobic digestion
(AD). Hydrolysis of biomass occurs naturally both under aerobic
and anaerobic conditions, but in the case of aerobic start, the pro-
duction of extracellular hydrolytic enzymes by facultative hydro-
lytic microbes increases by manifolds [40]. The presence of oxygen

promotes lignin oxidation due to microbial enzymes, which can
break down the polyphenolic polymer [20] and signiﬁcantly
improve the downstream biomethanation [29]. Thus the estab-
lishment of microaerobic conditions in the anaerobic digestion
process seems to be an appropriate solution that can improve the
hydrolysis step and boost biogas yield from lignocellulosic biomass
[41].
[29] found that the injection of two pulses 7.3 mL O2/g VS of
aeration on agricultural residues enhanced biomass hydrolysis and
resulted in a 9% enhanced biomethane yield for a treatment period
of 47 h. While increasing the dose to 15 mL O2/g VS hurt hydrolysis
and thus decreased methane yield. The optimization results of the
present study indicate that digester injected with a single injection
of 7.3 mL O2/g VS of the substrate for 12 h contact time degraded
78% acid-soluble lignin (ASL) and resulted in 32% enhancement of
the biogas yield.
The literature suggests the employment of microaeration for
short periods to achieve efﬁcient hydrolysis of organic material at
the beginning of the digestion process [33]. This would not only
enhance the hydrolysis of organic biomass but also promote the
acidogenesis step. On the contrary, a higher dosage of oxygen for an
extended period can inhibit methanogenic activity and gas yield
[21]. Accordingly, in the present study 7.3 mL O2/g VS aeration dose
resulted in higher lignin degradation for 12 h followed by 24 h
aeration contact times. For 12 h aeration contact time, 7.3 mL O2/g
VS dose resulted in 68% higher lignin degradation than the 5.3 mL
O2/g VS dose and 75% higher than the 9.3 mL O2/g VS dose. Simi-
larly, for 24 h aeration contact time, 7.3 mL O2/g VS dose resulted in
71% higher lignin degradation than the 5.3 mL O2/g VS dose and
65% higher than the 9.3 mL O2/g VS dose. Thus, in addition to the
suitable aeration dose (described in previous studies), the current
study also suggested suitable aeration contact time and aeration
frequency for the degradation of lignin.
3.2. Inﬂuence of microaeration pretreatment on biogas production
Based on the lignin degradation data collected in phase I, the
buffalo manure was pretreated with 7.3 mL O2/g VS aeration dose
for 12 h before phase II (anaerobic digestion) of this study. Pre-
treated buffalo manure was anaerobically digested at mesophilic
conditions (35 C) for 14 d. Fig. 4a compares the daily biogas yield of
pretreated (aerated) and untreated (unaerated) manure samples. In
both cases, the biogas production started on day 1. However, the
biogas yield of the aerated manure samples remained higher than
the unaerated manure samples for the ﬁrst 10 days of the digestion.
On average the daily biogas yield for the pretreated samples was
79 ± 9 mL biogas/g VS/d which was approximately 32% higher than
the control (54 ± 2 mL biogas/g VS/d). The biogas production ﬂat-
tened for both the treated samples and control after 10 d and did
not change signiﬁcantly thereafter. Overall, during 14 d digestion,
there was an accumulation of 1226 ± 53 mL of biogas in the treated
digesters whereas the untreated digesters accumulated only
900 ± 12 mL biogas (27% lesser than treated samples) as shown in
Fig. 4b.
The effectiveness of microaerobic pretreatment for the promo-
tion of hydrolysis and subsequent biogasiﬁcation has been estab-
lished by the literature. [29]; reported that biomethane production
increases by 9% with the injection of 7.3 mL O2/g VS aeration dose
for microaerobic pretreatment. Another study reported a 7%
enhancement in anaerobic digestion with the injection of 7.3 mL
O2/g VS [23]. Similarly, it was reported that the highest enhance-
ment in biogas production in wheat straw was obtained with
microaeration pretreatment of 5 mL O2/g VS [29]. However, the
effective aeration dose varies with the substrate. Table 4 shows the
effects of aeration doses and aeration contact times on the hydro-
lysis and biogas yield of different substrates reported in the
literature.
It can be seen in Table 4 that aeration can have both positive and
negative effects on the biogas yield. For instance, the agricultural
residues pretreated with 7.3 ml O2/g VS/day had a 7% enhancement
in biogas production while increasing the aeration dose to 15 ml O2/
g VS/day negatively impacted the process [23]. Similarly, insufﬁ-
cient microaerobic conditions showed decreased performance in
biogas yield. This might be due to hampering in production of the
enzymes for hydrolysis of biomass [33]. [28] reported that the

3.3. Total phenolics production, pH, total and volatile solids
reduction
Lignin is a complex polyphenolic biopolymer, and its degrada-
tion leads to the production of phenolic compounds [42]. Accord-
ingly, the concentration of total phenolics was measured to verify
the degradation of lignin due to aeration pretreatment as compared
to control. As illustrated in Fig. 5a, the concentration of total phe-
nolics of the microaerobically pretreated substrate was higher than
the control. This increase in total phenolics during aerobic pre-
treatment was found to have a positive effect on biogas yield during
anaerobic digestion as described in previous studies [43]. Another
important parameter that controls the performance of the AD
process is pH with an optimum range of 6e8.5 [44]. For the current
study, the pH of both the aerated and unaerated substrate remained
within the suitable range as shown in Fig. 5b. Buffalo manure

4. Conclusions
The current study demonstrated that a suitable combination of
aeration dose, aeration frequency, and aeration contact time
effectively enhanced the lignin degradation and thus the biogas
yield (p < 0.05). A single injection of 7.3 ml O2/g VS of the substrate
for 12 h contact time degraded 78% more acid-soluble lignin and
achieved a 32% increase in biogas yield on daily basis as compared
to the control. Increasing the aeration frequency or aeration dose
beyond 7.3 ml O2/g VS did not improve the lignin degradation. The
modiﬁed Gompertz model effectively predicted the kinetic pa-
rameters associated with biogas production under the given
experimental conditions process (R2 > 0.93). The ﬁndings of this
study advocate the use of a low-cost microaerobic pretreatment
strategy for the promotion of potential biomass to bioenergy pro-
jects in developing countries like Pakistan.
